title: Critical-risk governance is shifting toward anticipatory, whole-of-society preparedness, but learning, accountability and international coordination lag
source_unit: OECD, Tracking Progress in the Governance of Critical Risks
geography: 34 OECD countries adhering to the OECD Recommendation on the Governance of Critical Risks

denominator.unit: OECD countries surveyed against the Recommendation's five principles

implementation.value: most countries made progress across the five principles, but implementation remains uneven

risk_scope.value: national strategies increasingly address emerging climate risks, concurrent or multi-risk events, misinformation and disinformation impacts, and security of supply

observations.method: OECD survey and review of country implementation of the 2014 Recommendation, covering progress through 2023 and implementation context through 2024.
observations.uncertainty: The review measures governance arrangements and reported progress, not realized resilience, avoided losses or performance in a common crisis test.
observations.subgroup: National governments, subnational authorities, critical infrastructure operators, businesses, voluntary organizations and communities exposed to systemic risks.
observations.counterinterpretation: Formal strategies and institutions may coexist with weak operational capacity; broader risk language does not prove that governments can manage compound crises effectively.

observations.period: 2018-2024 implementation context; whole-of-government and whole-of-society coordination

consultation.value: all adherents have some consultative mechanisms, while whole-of-government coordination still needs improvement

partnerships.value: COVID-19 highlighted the need for regulatory flexibility, clear emergency authority with time limits and oversight, and incentives for private and voluntary-sector participation

social_cohesion.value: social cohesion and broad participation are treated as conditions for legitimate and durable risk governance

observations.method: Comparative governance review of country arrangements and lessons identified from recent crises.
observations.uncertainty: Consultation and partnership mechanisms vary in depth, representativeness and authority; their existence does not establish meaningful influence over decisions.
observations.subgroup: Public agencies, elected officials, firms, civil society, voluntary organizations and communities with different capacities to participate in emergency governance.
observations.counterinterpretation: A whole-of-society model can distribute responsibility and resources more effectively, but can also shift burdens onto communities or private actors without accountability or support.

observations.period: 2026 review; anticipation, foresight and preparedness investment

assessment_gap.value: risk assessments are common, but their connection to investment and preparedness decisions is uneven

foresight_gap.value: foresight and horizon scanning remain underdeveloped and weakly connected to operational decision-making

international_gap.value: international cooperation is recognized as essential but is among the least developed and exercised parts of risk-governance arrangements

observations.method: Synthesis of country survey responses and OECD assessment of risk identification, anticipation, prevention, preparedness and cross-border cooperation.
observations.uncertainty: The report identifies institutional gaps but does not quantify how much additional investment or cooperation would change crisis outcomes.
observations.subgroup: Risk analysts, finance and infrastructure planners, emergency managers, cross-border institutions and populations affected by cascading failures.
observations.counterinterpretation: Foresight is difficult to institutionalize because uncertainty, political time horizons and budget competition can make preventive benefits hard to demonstrate.

observations.period: 2026 review; transparency, accountability and systemic learning

accountability.value: transparency and accountability mechanisms remain scarce or weak in many systems

learning.value: most countries lack institutionalized, systematic learning from crises

emerging_dependencies.value: an updated framework may need to address emerging technologies, supply-chain fragility, geopolitical tensions and critical-infrastructure dependencies

observations.method: Comparative review of accountability, evaluation and learning arrangements, with implications for updating the OECD Recommendation.
observations.uncertainty: The report does not establish that weak formal accountability caused poor crisis outcomes or that an updated Recommendation would resolve these gaps.
observations.subgroup: Citizens, public servants, infrastructure users, firms, oversight bodies and communities that bear the consequences of opaque or poorly learned crisis decisions.
observations.counterinterpretation: Post-crisis learning can be politically constrained, but excessive proceduralization may also slow urgent decisions or obscure responsibility across complex systems.

boundary: This record adds a governance and geopolitical-risk signal: states are broadening risk frameworks toward compound threats, anticipatory planning, whole-of-society participation and critical dependencies, while accountability, learning, preparedness investment and cross-border cooperation lag. It is a comparative governance review, not a causal evaluation of resilience, a forecast of a specific crisis or proof that formal arrangements translate into public safety.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: The official OECD publication page and downloadable report were reviewed for the 34-country frame, five-principle progress assessment, whole-of-government and whole-of-society findings, anticipation and investment gaps, international cooperation, accountability, learning and emerging dependency implications.
